name: Romana Kuts
body:
Most B2B content was already bad before AI showed up. I'll say that as plainly as I said it the first time, because I still think it's the actual root of the problem everyone's currently blaming on AI.

Walk through ten B2B blogs in any category and count how many of them say anything a competitor couldn't have said with the names swapped. Before ChatGPT existed, that content was already generic, already optimized for a keyword instead of a reader, already written by someone with zero actual conversations with the buyer it was supposedly for. AI didn't create that problem. It just made it possible to produce the exact same generic content at ten times the volume, which is a considerably worse outcome, but not a new one.

I've led content teams at Leadfeeder and Dealfront, and I've seen this pattern up close from the inside: the blog posts that actually drove pipeline were never the ones optimized hardest for search volume. They were the ones written from an actual, specific point of view, usually pulled directly from a real sales call, a real customer objection, a real internal debate about how to position something. The ones that quietly underperformed were technically correct and said nothing anyone would remember an hour later.

What AI has actually done, and I think this part gets missed in most of the panic, is remove the excuse. It used to be genuinely expensive and slow to produce a lot of mediocre content, so mediocre content at least had scarcity working in its favor. Now mediocre content is nearly free to produce at scale, which means the only thing left to differentiate on is whether it was actually worth writing in the first place. That's a harder standard to hold yourself to than a word count or a keyword density target, and I think it's exactly the standard B2B content should have been held to all along.

I think about this every time a prospective client asks what makes SaaStorm different from the last agency they tried. The honest answer isn't a proprietary process or a secret framework. It's that we still hold every piece we ship to the same question a good editor would have asked before AI ever existed: does this actually deserve a reader's attention, or does it just fill a slot on the calendar. That question was always the right filter. AI just made it more urgent to actually apply it.

A specific example I still think about: a client's existing blog had a technically well-optimized article ranking reasonably well, built entirely around a keyword rather than an actual point of view. We didn't touch the SEO structure. We rewrote the argument underneath it, gave it a specific stance a competitor's version of the same article didn't have, and watched both rankings and time-on-page improve without changing a single technical element.

name: Romana Kuts
body:
I got sick for a few days recently, came back to LinkedIn, and half my feed had apparently mastered Claude, built entire automated systems, and shipped more in a week than I had in a month. My first instinct was the same one I think most of us have in that moment: quiet panic that everyone else had figured something out I hadn't.

Here's what I actually believe instead, and I think it's the most honest thing I can say about this exact moment in our industry: we're all figuring this out in real time. The pace right now is moving fast enough that experience only gives you pattern recognition, not a permanent lead. Five years of B2B content experience doesn't mean I automatically know the right AI workflow better than someone six months into their career who happened to experiment with the right tool last week.

That's a genuinely uncomfortable thing to admit publicly when your actual job title has 'expert' baked into how people perceive you. But I think pretending otherwise is worse, because it teaches everyone watching that falling behind for a week means you've permanently lost ground, when the honest reality is that the field is resetting constantly enough that this week's gap closes the moment you actually sit down and experiment.

My actual advice, the same thing I tell people I mentor: get a twenty dollar Claude subscription and build something for yourself first, before trying to formalize a workflow for a client. A content brief template for your own niche. A simple automation for something you already do manually every week. Not because it needs to be impressive. Because the only way pattern recognition actually forms is by building the pattern yourself, and no amount of watching someone else's LinkedIn post about their system gives you that the same way actually doing it does.

I've started saying this openly to clients too, not just on LinkedIn. When someone asks whether our team has fully mastered a specific new AI workflow, the honest answer is usually that we're testing it in real time alongside them, and I'd rather be transparent about that than perform a confidence that isn't real. Clients respond better to that honesty than I expected. Most of them are living the exact same uncertainty internally, and hearing an agency admit it plainly seems to build more trust, not less.

name: Romana Kuts
body:
We started doing something with client blog content that looked unnecessary the first time I suggested it: embedding a three-minute Loom video directly under the H1, a subject matter expert simply answering the core question of the article on camera, before a single paragraph of text.

The instinct to skip this is understandable. It's extra production work for an asset most people assume nobody will actually watch, competing against a reader who just wants to skim the article and leave. I'd have agreed with that instinct two years ago. What changed my mind wasn't a theory. It was watching engagement and time-on-page data for articles that had the video versus ones that didn't, across enough client accounts that it stopped looking like a coincidence.

Here's my actual read on why it works, beyond the raw numbers. A three-minute video from a real subject matter expert does something a paragraph of well-optimized text structurally cannot: it proves, immediately and unmistakably, that a real person who actually knows this topic is behind the content, rather than a generic byline attached to something that could have been assembled from other people's articles. In a search landscape where AI-generated content is flooding every category at volume, that proof of an actual human perspective is becoming one of the only differentiators left that's genuinely hard to fake convincingly.

It's also, honestly, not that expensive to produce once you build the habit. A subject matter expert doesn't need a script or a production crew. They need one focused question and three minutes to answer it in their own words, imperfections included. I'd rather ship a slightly rough three-minute video that proves a real person is behind the content than a flawlessly polished paragraph that could have come from anyone, anywhere, about anything.

We've since made this a standard part of how we brief content for clients with a real subject matter expert available, not an occasional experiment. It doesn't work for every piece, and I don't think it should. But for the pieces where a genuine point of view actually matters, having a real person say it on camera, imperfections included, has become one of the more reliably effective additions to our own playbook.

name: Joy Corkery
body:
A meaningful part of my actual job right now is evaluating AI-generated content for logical coherence, factual accuracy, and brand voice, across multiple client accounts at once. I want to be honest that this is a genuinely different skill than writing content from scratch, and it took me longer to build than I expected.

Writing from scratch, you catch problems as you create them, in real time, because you're the one making every decision. Evaluating something already written, especially something that reads fluently on a first pass, requires a different kind of attention: actively hunting for the specific place where a claim sounds plausible but isn't quite grounded in anything real, or where the logic of one paragraph quietly contradicts the paragraph two above it.

The failure mode I watch for most closely isn't obvious factual errors, which are usually easy to catch. It's confident, fluent-sounding filler dressed up as insight, a sentence that reads smoothly and says almost nothing specific, sitting comfortably next to sentences that do real work. AI is genuinely good at producing that kind of filler, because it's optimized to sound coherent, not to have earned every sentence's place in the piece.

What's actually helped me build this skill faster is treating every piece I evaluate against one specific question: could I explain, out loud, to the client, exactly why this specific sentence deserves to exist in this piece. If I can't answer that clearly for a given paragraph, it usually doesn't survive the edit, regardless of how fluent it reads. That discipline, more than any formal checklist, is what's made me faster and more confident evaluating content I didn't write myself.

The accounts where I've built this instinct fastest are the ones where I'm reviewing a high volume of similar content types repeatedly, since pattern recognition for what fluent filler looks like sharpens considerably faster with repetition than with a single careful read now and then. I'd rather build that instinct deliberately across a narrow set of formats than spread thin trying to evaluate everything with equal rigor from day one.

name: Joy Corkery
body:
I write detailed content briefs and editorial frameworks across multiple client accounts, and I've noticed the same misunderstanding come up often enough that I think it's worth addressing directly: most people think a content brief is a topic and a word count. It's closer to a decision document than an assignment.

A usable brief, in my experience, has to answer a specific question before a writer ever opens a blank page: what does this reader currently believe that's wrong or incomplete, and what do we want them to believe by the end of the piece. Without that, a writer is guessing at the actual point of the article, which usually produces something technically on-topic and genuinely unfocused, competent sentences that never quite build toward anything.

The other piece most briefs skip, and the one I've learned to never skip myself, is naming what NOT to include. Every topic in B2B SaaS has an obvious, well-covered angle that a dozen competitors have already written, and a brief that doesn't explicitly rule that angle out tends to get it anyway, because it's the path of least resistance for anyone writing under a deadline.

Getting this right takes longer at the brief stage than a simple topic-and-word-count document would. It saves considerably more time downstream, because a writer working from a genuinely clear brief rarely needs a full rewrite, just a polish pass. The alternative, a vague brief followed by heavy editing after the fact, costs more total time across the whole process. It just distributes that cost less visibly, spread across edits instead of concentrated upfront where it's easier to see.

I've started treating the 'what not to include' section of a brief as equally important as the topic itself, sometimes more so, because it's the part most writers genuinely appreciate once they see it in practice. It removes a decision they'd otherwise have to make alone, under deadline, usually by defaulting to whatever's easiest to write rather than what actually serves the piece.

name: Joy Corkery
body:
A lot of the conversation around LLM optimisation right now frames it as a replacement for technical SEO, a newer discipline that makes the older one obsolete. Working across multiple client accounts applying both at once, I don't think that framing holds up, and I want to explain why with something more specific than a general disagreement.

Traditional SEO and LLM visibility are answering genuinely different questions, even when they look related on the surface. Traditional SEO is largely about whether your specific page ranks for a specific query, structure, keywords, technical crawlability, backlinks. LLM optimisation is closer to whether your brand shows up, correctly and favorably, inside a synthesized answer that might never link back to your page at all. A page can be technically excellent by every SEO standard and still be invisible to an LLM that's pulling its answer from a different set of sources entirely, ones that happen to mention your brand more consistently across the web.

What I've actually found working both disciplines together is that they compound rather than compete. The technical SEO fundamentals, clean structure, genuine expertise, real internal linking, still matter enormously for how crawlable and trustworthy your content looks to any system evaluating it, human or AI. LLM-specific tactics, being mentioned accurately across third-party sources, structuring content around the actual questions people ask an AI assistant rather than the queries they'd type into Google, add on top of that foundation rather than replacing it.

The accounts where I've seen the strongest combined results are the ones where we didn't choose between the two disciplines. We kept the technical SEO work rigorous and layered LLM-specific structuring on top of content that was already earning its place for human readers and search engines both.

The accounts where this combined approach has worked best are the ones where the client's own team understood early that this wasn't an either-or decision to make once and move on from. It's an ongoing balance that shifts slightly as both disciplines keep evolving, and treating it as settled too early is its own kind of risk.

name: Michelle Newblom
body:
My degree is in Creative Writing, which is not the credential most people expect from someone writing SEO blogs and long-form guides for B2B SaaS companies. I get asked about that gap often enough that I think it's worth answering properly rather than brushing past it.

What a Creative Writing program actually teaches, underneath the workshops and the fiction assignments, is a genuinely transferable instinct: reading a piece of writing and immediately sensing where it drags, where a sentence is doing decoration instead of work, where the structure is fighting the point instead of supporting it. That instinct doesn't care whether the piece is a short story or a SaaS feature comparison guide. A paragraph that's technically correct and boring to read fails for the same underlying reason in both.

What I had to build separately, and what no creative writing workshop prepared me for, was the actual mechanics of B2B content: understanding a buying committee, writing toward a specific stage of a funnel, structuring a piece so it satisfies both a skimming reader and a search engine at once. That took real, deliberate learning, working across clients like Cerby, Toggl, and Codeless Interactive, watching what actually drove engagement versus what just read nicely.

I think the honest lesson for anyone with a similarly unconventional background wondering if it translates is that the craft instinct genuinely does transfer, and the domain knowledge genuinely doesn't, automatically. You still have to build the second half deliberately. But starting with the first half already in place is a real advantage, even if it takes a while to recognize it as one rather than a mismatch you need to explain away in every interview.

I think the honest advice I'd give someone earlier in a similarly unconventional path is to stop treating the mismatch as something to explain away in an interview and start treating it as an actual asset worth naming directly. The moment I stopped apologizing for the Creative Writing degree and started explaining specifically what it gave me, the conversation in interviews changed considerably.

name: Michelle Newblom
body:
I spent time as a Content Marketing Associate at WRITER, which meant writing about AI-assisted writing itself, for an audience of people evaluating whether AI-assisted writing tools were actually worth trusting. That's a strange, slightly recursive position to write from, and it taught me something I still apply to every client account since.

Writing about a category from inside a company selling into that exact category requires a specific kind of restraint most content doesn't need. It's tempting to lean on the same confident, slightly oversold language every competitor in the category uses, because it's the path of least resistance and it's what the category has trained readers to expect. The actual differentiator, I found, was writing with more precision and less certainty than the category default, being specific about exactly where a tool or approach helps and where it genuinely doesn't, rather than defaulting to blanket confidence.

That restraint is harder to write than it sounds, because it means resisting a sentence that would sound more impressive in exchange for one that's more honestly scoped. I remember cutting a claim from an early draft that would have made a feature sound more capable than it actually was in practice, replacing it with a narrower, less flashy but fully accurate description. The piece read slightly less exciting. It also held up under scrutiny from a reader who actually tested the tool afterward, which the flashier version wouldn't have.

I carry that instinct into every B2B SaaS account I write for now: the version of a claim that's slightly less impressive but fully defensible almost always serves a reader, and the client, better over time than the version that oversells by a small, easily-forgiven-in-the-moment margin.

That restraint has become something close to a personal editing rule now, applied well beyond just AI-adjacent content. Before a sentence goes out under a client's name, I ask whether it would survive a reader who tested the actual claim afterward. If I'm not confident it would, it gets rewritten narrower, even when the narrower version reads slightly less impressive in isolation.

name: Michelle Newblom
body:
Before moving fully into B2B SaaS content, I worked as an editor at LexBlog, editing legal industry content written by genuine subject matter experts, lawyers, who were brilliant at their actual field and not necessarily trained writers. That role taught me an editing instinct I still rely on constantly: the job isn't to make every piece sound like it came from the same voice. It's to protect whatever specific, genuine insight the writer actually has, and clear away whatever's getting in its way.

The temptation as an editor, especially early in that role, is to smooth every piece toward a consistent, polished house style, because consistency is easier to manage across many contributors. I learned quickly that flattening a genuine subject matter expert's slightly rougher, more specific voice into generic polish often cost the piece its actual value. A lawyer's slightly unusual way of framing a specific legal nuance was frequently the most useful sentence in the entire piece, and over-editing toward smoothness was the fastest way to quietly delete it.

What I actually did instead, once I recognized this, was edit for clarity and structure while deliberately preserving the specific phrasing that carried real expertise, even when it didn't match a generic house style perfectly. That meant more editorial judgment call by call, rather than a single consistent rule applied uniformly across every piece.

I bring that same instinct into B2B SaaS content now, especially when working from a subject matter expert's interview or notes. The goal isn't to make their insight sound like every other piece on the blog. It's to protect the specific thing they actually know that a generic writer wouldn't, and build the piece around preserving that rather than smoothing it away.

I still think about that lawyer's specific phrasing sometimes, years later, as a kind of internal benchmark. Whatever I'm editing now, client content, my own drafts, I ask whether I'm protecting the one sentence that actually carries real expertise, or quietly smoothing it into something that reads more consistently and says less.

name: Beth Colman
body:
I'd been quietly admiring SaaStorm's content for a long time before I ever applied to join the team, and I want to be specific about what actually drew me in, rather than leave it as a vague compliment.

A lot of agency content reads like it was written to satisfy a keyword requirement first and a reader second. What I kept noticing scrolling through SaaStorm's blog and Romana's own LinkedIn posts was the opposite ordering: a real, specific point of view stated plainly, with the SEO structure clearly built around that point rather than the point squeezed awkwardly into a structure decided in advance. Romana's content specifically was a big part of what pulled me in, the directness of it, the willingness to say something a reader might actually disagree with rather than something safely agreeable.

What made me want to actually apply, rather than just keep admiring from a distance, was realizing how much of my own instinct as a writer had been quietly dulled by writing to satisfy briefs that prioritized safety over specificity. I'd gotten good at producing competent, inoffensive content, and I'd started to notice that competence and genuine usefulness to a reader had drifted apart in my own work without me fully choosing that drift.

Joining a team where writing is treated as the actual product, not a delivery mechanism for keywords, has already changed how I approach a first draft. I'm asking earlier now what I actually believe about a topic before I ask what the brief requires, which is a small reordering that's made a real difference in how the writing reads. I'm genuinely excited to focus on writing again, in the way I mean that word, rather than content production that happens to use full sentences.

I've since gone back and reread some of those early admired posts with a slightly different eye, trying to reverse-engineer exactly what made them land the way they did. What I keep finding is less a formula than a consistent willingness to commit to a specific claim rather than hedge it, which is a harder habit to build than any structural technique a style guide could teach.

name: Beth Colman
body:
My first brief at SaaStorm surprised me, and I want to explain why, because I think it reveals something about how this team actually approaches content that's different from most places I've written for before.

The brief didn't just specify a topic and an audience. It specified, explicitly, a position we were taking that a reasonable competitor would disagree with, and asked me to write toward defending that position clearly rather than covering the topic neutrally from all sides. I'd been trained, across a lot of previous B2B writing work, to hedge toward balance by default, presenting multiple perspectives so no reader could accuse the piece of being one-sided.

Writing toward an actual stated position instead was uncomfortable at first, in a way that told me something about how much safety-hedging had crept into my own default writing instincts without me choosing it deliberately. It's genuinely easier to write a balanced overview that offends nobody. It's harder, and more useful to an actual reader trying to make a decision, to write a piece that commits to a specific view and explains the reasoning clearly enough that even someone who disagrees understands exactly why you landed where you did.

The piece that came out of that brief performed better than I expected, and better than the safer, more neutral version I'd have defaulted to without that direction. I think the actual lesson, one I'm still internalizing a few weeks in, is that a reader trying to solve a real problem usually wants a clear answer more than a balanced survey of options, even when the clear answer means someone, somewhere, might push back on it.

I've since started applying that same instinct earlier in my own drafting process, asking myself before I write a paragraph whether I'm about to hedge toward safety out of habit rather than because the topic genuinely calls for balance. It's a small check that's already changed how a few pieces have turned out.

I think what made it land, more than the specific position itself, was the confidence that came from having actual reasoning behind it rather than just an opinion asserted flatly. Once I understood why we were taking that stance, defending it in the writing itself became considerably easier than I expected going in.

name: Beth Colman
body:
A few weeks into this role, I want to write honestly about what I'm actually paying attention to right now, rather than a polished summary of everything I've supposedly already mastered, because I think the honest version is more useful to anyone else starting somewhere new.

The thing I'm watching most closely isn't the writing mechanics themselves, which I already had a real foundation in before joining. It's the specific judgment calls that don't show up in any style guide: which claims need a source cited inline versus which are safe to state plainly based on general industry knowledge, how directly to state an opinion in a piece written for a client's brand voice versus one written under SaaStorm's own name, when a technically accurate sentence is still the wrong sentence because it doesn't serve where the reader actually is in their decision.

Those calls take real repetition to build good instincts for, and I don't think there's a shortcut around simply making enough of them, including the ones I'll get wrong along the way, to develop a reliable feel for where the line actually sits. I'd rather be honest about being in that building phase now than perform a confidence I don't fully have yet.

What's made this stretch genuinely enjoyable rather than just effortful is a team that treats a rough early draft as a normal part of the process rather than a problem to be quietly disappointed by. Getting real, specific feedback on where a piece isn't landing yet, rather than vague encouragement or silent correction, is exactly the kind of environment that actually builds the judgment I'm still working on faster than figuring it out alone would.

I'd rather be honest about still building that judgment than pretend I've already got a fully reliable feel for it after a few weeks. I think that honesty is actually more useful to anyone else early in a similar role than a polished account of instincts I haven't fully earned yet.

A few weeks from now I expect this list of judgment calls to look different, probably shorter in some places and longer in others as I find new categories of decision I hadn't noticed needed real thought yet. I'm treating that as a normal part of the ramp rather than a sign I should already have it fully mapped.

name: Rebekah Prime
body:
Six years managing copy and research at a B2B revenue intelligence company taught me something I don't think gets said plainly enough in most content marketing advice: the research phase is where most content quietly fails, long before a single sentence gets written.

A writer handed a topic and told to go write about it will produce something competent and generic almost by default, because competent and generic is what you get when the research underneath a piece is thin. The pieces that actually converted, in my experience managing that function, were never the ones with the cleverest headlines. They were the ones built on research specific enough that the writer had something genuinely new to say, a data point, a customer pattern, an industry shift nobody else had bothered to actually verify before writing about it.

What that meant practically, running a research function at scale, was resisting the pressure to move writers to drafting faster. Every piece that skipped a proper research pass in favor of speed came back for more revision later, which is a slower total process dressed up as a faster one. The pieces where research got genuine time upfront needed far less rework once drafting started, because the writer already had real material to build from rather than padding a thin premise with confident-sounding filler.

I carry that discipline into every piece I write now, whether it's a blog article, a white paper, or email copy. The actual differentiator between content that converts and content that doesn't usually isn't visible in the finished piece at all. It's in the research decision made well before a single word got written, whether the writer found something genuinely specific to say or settled for a competent version of what everyone else in the category already says.

I still apply this same discipline to my own work now as a writer rather than a manager overseeing other writers' research. Before I let myself start drafting, I ask whether I've actually found something specific enough to say, or whether I'm about to write a competent, generic version of what the topic usually gets. If it's the second, I go back to research rather than push forward on a weak foundation.

name: Rebekah Prime
body:
Fifteen years writing across B2B and B2C, and the specific failure mode of a rushed piece looks genuinely different depending on the format, which I think gets flattened too often into a single generic complaint about quality.

A rushed case study fails by staying vague exactly where it needs to be specific, a client quote that could apply to any vendor, a results section that says 'significant improvement' instead of naming the actual number, because getting the specific detail required a follow-up conversation nobody had time to schedule. A rushed white paper fails differently: it tends to over-explain the obvious and under-explain the genuinely difficult part, because the obvious part is faster to write confidently and the hard part requires research the deadline didn't allow for. A rushed playbook fails worst of all the formats, in my experience, because a playbook that's vague at a specific step doesn't just underperform, it actively wastes the reader's time trying to execute a step that was never actually detailed enough to follow.

Knowing which specific failure mode a format is prone to has changed how I push back on unrealistic timelines. I don't just say a deadline is too tight in the abstract. I can usually name, specifically, which part of that particular format is going to suffer first if we don't protect enough time for it, the client quote that'll stay generic, the difficult section that'll get glossed over, the step that'll stay too vague to execute.

That specificity tends to land better in a timeline conversation than a general complaint about rushing ever does, because it gives whoever's setting the deadline something concrete to actually weigh against the schedule, rather than a vague quality concern easy to overrule under pressure.

I've started sharing this specific framing with clients directly when a timeline gets tight, rather than leaving it as an internal note to myself. Naming exactly which failure mode we're risking, rather than a general quality warning, tends to get a more serious response from whoever's setting the deadline, because it's concrete enough to actually weigh against the schedule pressure.

name: Rebekah Prime
body:
My undergraduate degree combined English Literature with Drama and Theatre Studies, which is not the background most people expect behind someone writing B2B case studies and playbooks now. But the theatre half specifically taught me something about structure I still use in every case study I write.

A play doesn't work by stating its theme directly. It works by building specific scenes that make the audience feel the theme without ever being told it outright, and the writer's job is deciding exactly which scene to show and which to skip, because showing every scene would bury the actual story in noise. I think about a B2B case study almost exactly the same way now: the client's actual challenge, the specific turning point, the concrete result, told through the fewest scenes that still make the arc land clearly, rather than a chronological account of everything that happened across the entire engagement.

Most case studies I read from other companies make the opposite mistake theatre training would flag immediately: they include every phase of the engagement in equal detail, which flattens the actual story into a timeline rather than a narrative with an actual shape. The reader can't tell which part mattered most, because everything is presented with the same weight.

What I do differently now, deliberately, is pick the one or two moments in a client engagement that actually carry the story, the specific decision point, the moment a metric visibly shifted, and build the entire case study around making that moment land clearly, cutting everything else down to the minimum context needed to understand it. It's a smaller, more selective structure than most case studies use. It's also, I think, the actual reason the ones I write tend to hold a reader's attention past the first paragraph.

I think the theatre training's biggest gift, in hindsight, wasn't really about case studies specifically. It was learning that a story earns attention through selection, not inclusion, and that lesson has turned out to apply to nearly every format I've written since, not just the ones that obviously resemble a narrative.

name: Jacob Collins
body:
Before writing content full time, I spent time consulting on marketing and go-to-market strategy, and I think that background shows up in my writing in a specific way most content writers without it don't have: I write content differently when I actually understand the GTM motion it's supposed to support.

A writer without strategy context tends to treat every piece as a standalone assignment, optimized for its own topic in isolation. Understanding the actual go-to-market motion behind a piece changes the questions you ask before writing a word: is this content meant to catch someone early, still forming their sense of the problem, or someone already comparing vendors and looking for a reason to choose one over another. Those are genuinely different pieces of writing, even when they're nominally about the same topic, and a writer who doesn't know which stage they're writing for tends to produce something that awkwardly tries to serve both at once and fully satisfies neither.

I've also found that understanding pipeline mechanics changes how I handle a call to action. A lot of content writing treats the CTA as an afterthought bolted onto the end of a piece, generic and interchangeable across every article on a site. Knowing the actual GTM motion means understanding what a reader at this specific stage is actually ready to do next, which is rarely 'book a demo' if they're still three steps away from being ready for that conversation.

I think the broader lesson, for any content writer without a strategy background, is that understanding the actual business motion a piece supports changes more about how you write it than any pure craft skill does. The sentences might read identically well either way. Only one version is actually built to move a specific reader toward a specific next step.

I've started asking a version of this funnel-stage question explicitly in every brief I write now, rather than assuming a writer will infer it correctly from context. It adds one extra line to the brief and saves considerably more time than it costs, since a writer working from an explicit answer rarely produces the awkward, trying-to-serve-everyone piece that comes from guessing.

name: Jacob Collins
body:
By the time a content calendar exists, with topics and dates and assigned writers, a considerable amount of strategic work has usually already happened invisibly, and I think that invisible work is where a lot of content programs actually succeed or fail, long before anyone's judging the finished articles.

The specific work I mean is deciding which topics genuinely deserve a place on the calendar at all, versus which ones sound reasonable in a brainstorm but don't actually map to anything a real buyer is trying to solve at a specific stage of their journey. That filtering work is unglamorous and easy to skip under time pressure, which is exactly why so many content calendars end up full of topics that are individually fine and collectively directionless, no clear throughline connecting why this specific set of articles, in this specific order, actually builds toward something.

My own background in GTM strategy consulting shapes how I do this filtering now. Before a topic earns a calendar slot, I try to answer a specific question: which stage of the actual buying journey does this serve, and what should a reader who's just consumed it be more ready to do afterward than they were before. A topic that can't answer that clearly, however interesting it sounds in isolation, usually doesn't survive the cut, regardless of how easy it would be to write.

That discipline costs real time upfront, time that could otherwise go straight into drafting. I think it's time well spent, because a content calendar built without that filtering tends to produce individually competent articles that never quite compound into anything, and a calendar that's done this filtering properly tends to feel, to a reader moving through several pieces over time, like it's actually leading somewhere on purpose.

I think the honest tension here is that this filtering work is genuinely unglamorous compared to the actual writing, and it's tempting to shortcut it when the calendar needs filling under deadline pressure. I've had to build real discipline around protecting that filtering step specifically because it's the one most likely to get quietly skipped when things get busy.

The accounts where I've seen this filtering skipped most often aren't the ones with weak strategists. They're the ones under the most calendar pressure, where the temptation to fill next week's slot with whatever sounds reasonable in the moment quietly overrides the discipline to ask whether it actually belongs there at all.

name: Jacob Collins
body:
I've worked alongside plenty of genuinely skilled writers who struggle specifically in B2B SaaS content, not because their writing is weak, but because of a specific, narrower gap I think is worth naming directly: understanding the actual mechanics of how a SaaS company generates and moves pipeline.

A skilled writer without that context can produce a genuinely well-written piece that's still strategically misplaced, addressing the wrong stage of the funnel, answering a question the actual target account already knows the answer to, or missing the specific objection that's actually stalling deals in the sales team's real conversations this quarter. The prose can be excellent and the piece can still fail at its actual job, because the job was never really about prose quality alone.

What closes that gap, in my experience, isn't more writing practice. It's direct exposure to the actual GTM motion: sitting in on sales calls, reading the specific objections showing up in the CRM this month, understanding which accounts are stalling and why, rather than working purely from a content calendar assigned by someone else further upstream. That exposure changes what a writer notices as relevant, even when nobody's explicitly telling them to write differently.

I think this is the actual argument for content writers spending real time close to sales and strategy conversations, not because craft doesn't matter, but because craft applied to the wrong strategic target still misses. The best B2B SaaS content I've seen combines strong writing with genuine proximity to how the business actually generates revenue, and I don't think either half substitutes for the other.

What's made the biggest difference in closing this gap for writers I've worked alongside isn't a training document explaining GTM concepts abstractly. It's direct, repeated exposure to the actual conversations happening in sales and strategy meetings, until the relevant questions start showing up in their own thinking without anyone having to prompt for them.

name: Jamie Adams
body:
I spent time leading SEO strategy, content strategy, and client management simultaneously across multiple accounts, and I want to describe what that actually looks like week to week, because from outside it can sound like three separate jobs stitched together, and it mostly isn't.

The reality is that these three functions constantly inform each other in ways that make treating them as separate workstreams actively counterproductive. An SEO insight about which topics are genuinely winnable this quarter directly changes what belongs on a content calendar. A client conversation about a shifting business priority directly changes which keywords are actually worth chasing versus which ones would technically rank but serve nobody the business currently cares about. Treating these as three handoffs between three specialists tends to lose exactly the information that matters most in the handoff itself.

What actually made this workable at scale wasn't a more sophisticated process. It was keeping a tight enough loop between strategy and execution that a shift in one didn't sit unaddressed for weeks before reaching the other. A keyword opportunity spotted on a Tuesday that doesn't reach the content calendar until the following sprint planning has usually gone stale by the time anyone acts on it, especially in a category moving as fast as B2B SaaS currently is.

I think the honest lesson from running this across several accounts at once is that the actual skill isn't mastering SEO, content, and client management as separate disciplines. It's maintaining a fast enough loop between them that an insight in one doesn't sit disconnected from the others long enough to lose its relevance, which is a coordination skill more than a technical one, and one I don't think gets nearly enough credit in how these roles usually get described.

I think the reason this coordination skill gets underrated is that it's genuinely hard to point to in a resume or a case study the way a specific SEO win or a specific piece of content can be. It shows up as the absence of a problem, campaigns that stayed aligned, insights that reached the right team before they went stale, which is much harder to showcase than a single impressive result.

name: Jamie Adams
body:
Part of my role involved AI workflow experimentation and internal marketing innovation, testing new tools and approaches before recommending them more broadly across client accounts. I want to be specific about what actually made that experimentation useful, because a lot of AI workflow experimentation right now produces a lot of activity and very little that's actually reliable enough to recommend.

The mistake I see most often, and the one I had to deliberately avoid in my own testing, is evaluating a new AI tool or workflow based on how impressive a single output looks. A workflow that produces one genuinely great result out of five attempts isn't a reliable workflow yet, even though the one great output is what tends to get shared and celebrated internally. What actually matters for recommending something more broadly is the consistency across attempts, not the ceiling of the best one.

What made my own experimentation actually useful to the team was building a real feedback loop before recommending anything: running the same workflow across a meaningful sample of real client scenarios, not a single cherry-picked example, and being honest about the failure rate alongside the successes. A workflow with a genuine seventy percent success rate that I'm transparent about is more useful to recommend than one presented as flawless based on its best single output, because the team adopting it needs to know where it'll need a human check, not just where it shines.

I think this discipline, treating internal AI experimentation with the same rigor as any other tested process rather than showcasing best-case demos, is what actually separates useful internal innovation from activity that looks impressive in a team meeting and quietly falls apart the first time someone tries to rely on it for a real deadline.

I've since built a habit of documenting the failure rate alongside every recommendation I make internally, even when it feels slightly deflating compared to just showcasing the best output. I think that honesty has actually made my recommendations land with more credibility over time, not less, because the team trusts that what I'm recommending has actually been tested rather than cherry-picked.

name: Jamie Adams
body:
I spent real time on quality assurance across client content, and I want to draw a distinction I think gets collapsed too often: quality assurance and editing are related but genuinely different jobs, and treating them as the same task tends to produce weaker output on both fronts.

Editing, as I think about it, is fundamentally about making a specific piece better: sharper sentences, tighter structure, a clearer argument. Quality assurance is a different question entirely: does this piece meet the standard we've committed to for this specific client, consistently, the same way the last fifty pieces did, regardless of who wrote it or how much time they had this week. An editor can make a mediocre piece meaningfully better and still miss that it violates a client-specific rule about how competitors get referenced. A QA pass exists specifically to catch that second kind of miss, one editing alone doesn't reliably catch because it's not editing's actual job.

What I built into my own QA process, once I recognized this distinction clearly, was a checklist genuinely separate from editorial judgment: factual claims verified against source material, brand and terminology consistency checked against each specific client's actual guidelines, formatting and structure checked against what that account has committed to delivering. None of that requires literary judgment. All of it requires actually checking rather than assuming a skilled writer got it right by default.

The accounts where quality stayed most consistent over time were never the ones with the most talented individual writers. They were the ones where QA ran as a genuinely separate step from editing, catching the specific, checkable things a talented writer focused on making the piece read well can easily miss simply because reading well and meeting every specific commitment aren't actually the same test.

I think the accounts I'm proudest of, looking back, were never the ones where a single writer's talent carried the work. They were the ones where the QA process caught the small, specific things a talented writer focused on the writing itself would understandably miss, simply because catching them was never really their job in the first place.

name: SaaStorm
body:
Working as in-house B2B marketers before starting SaaStorm, we dealt with a lot of marketing and SEO agencies, hoping they'd help us hit our actual goals. Most of them missed the mark, focused on vanity metrics like traffic and impressions instead of what actually matters: revenue, sign-ups, and high-quality leads. So we decided to do it better ourselves.

That's genuinely the whole founding story. Not a market gap identified through research, a frustration lived through directly, repeatedly, across enough agency relationships that the pattern became impossible to ignore. Agencies that reported impressive-looking dashboards while the actual pipeline conversation with sales stayed exactly as difficult as it was before the engagement started.

We built SaaStorm specifically to be revenue-driven from day one, tracking MQLs, SQLs, CAC, LTV, and pipeline revenue impact rather than the vanity metrics we'd been sold on ourselves in previous agency relationships. It's a harder standard to hold every piece of content and every campaign to, because it removes the easy win of a traffic chart trending upward regardless of whether that traffic converts into anything a sales team can actually use.

That's still the actual filter every SaaStorming session runs through today. Not does this idea sound clever, but does this idea move a real number that a client's CFO would actually recognize as meaningful. We'd rather be the agency that says no to an impressive-sounding vanity campaign than the one we used to hire ourselves, the one that looked great in a monthly report and never quite showed up in the pipeline.

We still return to that exact founding frustration whenever a SaaStorming session starts drifting toward an idea that sounds clever but wouldn't actually move a number a client's own leadership would recognize as meaningful. It's a useful filter precisely because it's specific and lived, not abstract, and it's held up for us the same way it apparently didn't for the agencies we used to hire ourselves.

name: SaaStorm
body:
20 million-plus in organic traffic delivered for clients. Over 1,000 SQLs generated, all warm leads, zero fluff. $30 million-plus in revenue fueled by our content strategies. Five million-plus words written, enough to power a small library. Those are the numbers we actually track, and we think they say more about what we do than any tagline could.

We also keep a sillier set of numbers, because we think the discipline of revenue-focused marketing doesn't have to mean humorless marketing. Over 10,000 cups of coffee consumed, which we like to think of as creative fuel. Roughly 1,238,930 hours spent perfecting client strategies, approximately, but who's counting. 404-plus growth opportunities uncovered, because we don't miss a thing. 301-plus 'meh' ideas redirected into brilliance during our own internal SaaStorming sessions.

We track both sets deliberately. The serious numbers are the actual proof that revenue-focused marketing works at scale, across 50-plus B2B SaaS growth teams of every size. The sillier numbers are a reminder, mostly to ourselves, that a team obsessed with pipeline revenue and CAC ratios can still enjoy the actual work, and that the two things aren't in tension the way a lot of agency culture seems to assume they are.

We'd rather be the team clients describe as an extension of their own, not a vendor delivering a monthly report. The numbers above are what that actually adds up to, measured honestly, tracked consistently, and occasionally counted with a sense of humor about just how many cups of coffee it took to get there.

We update both sets of numbers regularly, and we've noticed something worth naming: the serious numbers tend to get shared by prospective clients evaluating us, and the sillier ones tend to get shared by our own team internally, on a slow week, as a small reminder of how much has actually accumulated over time. We think both kinds of sharing matter, for different reasons.

We've thought about retiring the sillier stats more than once, worried they might undercut the seriousness of the real numbers sitting right next to them. So far the opposite has been true. Prospective clients mention the coffee count almost as often as the revenue figure when they tell us what made them remember us.

name: SaaStorm
body:
Every new engagement at SaaStorm starts with a two-week discovery phase, no strings attached. At the end of it, a prospective client can choose to partner with us, or take the results and run with them entirely on their own. We get asked fairly often why we'd structure things this way, effectively giving away real, usable work before any contract is signed.

The honest answer is that we think it's the only fair test of whether a revenue-focused marketing claim actually holds up under scrutiny. It's easy for any agency to promise results in a sales conversation. It's a considerably higher bar to deliver something genuinely useful in the first two weeks, before any long-term commitment exists to soften the standard we're holding ourselves to.

We've had prospective clients take those two weeks of work and go execute it themselves, without ever becoming a paying client, and we've made peace with that as an acceptable outcome of the model rather than a failure of it. If two weeks of real, honest work convinces a team they don't need us, that's a more honest signal than a longer sales cycle built on promises rather than delivered work would have given either of us.

What this structure actually protects, more than anything, is the quality of the engagements that do convert. A client who partners with us after seeing genuinely useful work firsthand, rather than after being sold on a pitch deck, tends to have realistic expectations about what we can actually deliver, which makes for a considerably healthier working relationship over the following months than one built on a promise that hasn't yet been tested against real output.

We've had a few internal debates about whether giving away two weeks of real, usable work for free is simply too generous a model to sustain at scale. So far, the conversion quality from prospects who've seen real output first has more than justified the occasional walk-away, and we'd rather protect that quality than chase a slightly higher close rate built on less proof upfront.

name: SaaStorm
body:
We've published three detailed success stories so far, Lingio, Reditus, and OneUp, and I want to talk about what actually connects them, because it's not the tactics, it's a specific starting condition each of them shared.

Lingio grew organic traffic by 500% in 9 months, leading to an 11x increase in inbound leads. Reditus, fully bootstrapped, built a $1.3M ARR pipeline with 128% inbound pipeline growth and over 100 sales opportunities. OneUp scaled a consistent flow of high-intent traffic into a content engine that supported over £250K in inbound revenue, with 711% year-over-year growth in blog clicks alone.

Three different companies, three different categories, three different starting points. What they actually had in common wasn't a shared tactic we rolled out identically across all three. It was a willingness to commit to content as an actual growth channel long enough for compounding to show up, rather than judging the engine after one quarter and pulling the plug when the traffic chart hadn't yet turned into a pipeline chart.

That's the part of these stories that doesn't fit neatly into a single stat on a case study page. SEO and content-led growth typically take 3 to 6 months to show substantial results, and every one of these three teams stayed the course through the part of that timeline where the work is happening but the dashboard doesn't yet reflect it. We track MQLs, SQLs, CAC, LTV, and pipeline revenue specifically because that's what proves the commitment was worth it in the end, not the vanity traffic number that looks good in month two and means nothing if it never becomes a number sales can actually use.

If you're evaluating whether content-led growth is worth committing to, the honest answer is that it works, repeatedly, across genuinely different B2B SaaS categories, but only for teams willing to measure it on the timeline it actually operates on rather than the one a paid campaign would.

We're aware that three published stories is a modest sample size to draw a firm conclusion from, and we'd rather say that plainly than oversell the pattern. What we can say honestly is that the pattern has held for every account we've had the runway to work with long enough to actually measure, which is itself a useful signal about what 'long enough' actually requires in this category.
